In this case, the corresponding index is known as the “half-index” (of Neumann boundary condition) [14]. Due to an obvious symmetry between *t* and *u*, the limit *t →* 0 is essentially same as *u →* 0. However, in the analysis in the next subsection, these two limits look different, and lead to the equivalent result non-trivially. Finally, if we set *u* = *q/t*, the resulting index is known as the flavored Schur index. The single letter index is now given by

As mentioned in the introductory section, we refer to *IN*(*t,u*; *q*) as the deformed Schur index.
